sentenceSets.sentence: The new terminology had become ubiquitous within eighteen months, which made it impossible to determine whether the ideas behind it had actually spread.

answerChoices.reasoning: Popular (liked or enjoyed by many) describes adoption but lacks the sense of being everywhere at the same time.
Widespread (existing or occurring over a large area or number) is very similar but is less about simultaneous presence everywhere.
Pervasive (spreading or existing throughout) is close but emphasizes thorough diffusion rather than constant simultaneous presence.
Dominant (most important or prevalent) describes prevalence but not the quality of being everywhere at once.
Common (happening or found often) involves frequency but not the sense of being everywhere simultaneously.
Fashionable (currently popular or in fashion) involves temporary adoption but not universal presence.
Endemic (regularly occurring in a particular place) is location-specific, unlike ubiquitous.
Rare (seldom occurring or found) is opposite to being everywhere.
Localized (restricted to a particular place) is contrary to being everywhere at the same time.
Sporadic (occurring occasionally) opposes the constant, simultaneous presence.
Obscure (not widely known or unknown) is opposite to ubiquitous presence.

sentenceSets.sentence: Smartphones had become ubiquitous, so the sight of someone without one had grown genuinely peculiar, almost alarming.

answerChoices.reasoning: Universal (applicable to all cases) is similar but emphasizes total inclusion rather than present everywhere simultaneously.
Omnipresent (present everywhere at the same time) is nearly identical but is more formal and literary.
Inescapable (impossible to avoid) overlaps but emphasizes unavoidability rather than physical presence everywhere.
Standard (normal or expected) describes commonness but not the sense of being present everywhere.
Common (happening frequently) involves frequency but not the simultaneous universal presence.
Ordinary (commonplace) describes normalcy but not universal simultaneous presence.
Typical (characteristic of a type) involves expectation but not the everywhere-at-once quality.
Unique (being the only one) is opposite to universal presence.
Rare (seldom found) is contrary to presence everywhere.
Absent (not present) is opposite to ubiquitous presence.
Occasional (happening from time to time) opposes the constant everywhere presence.

sentenceSets.sentence: The composer's motif was so ubiquitous throughout the symphony that listeners could not tell whether its familiarity arose from genius or from mere repetition.

answerChoices.reasoning: Recurring (happening again and again) involves repetition but does not capture the sense of being everywhere throughout the work.
Persistent (continuing firmly despite difficulty) involves constancy but emphasizes stubborn duration rather than omnipresence.
Repetitive (repeated many times) describes the frequency but lacks the sense of simultaneous presence everywhere in the piece.
Relentless (continuing without pause or yielding) involves constancy but emphasizes intensity rather than omnipresence.
Constant (unchanged and unvarying) involves continuous presence but is less specific to the everywhere-at-once quality.
Unremitting (never stopping) emphasizes duration but not the sense of presence everywhere.
Abundant (existing in large quantities) involves plenty but not the everywhere-at-once quality.
Rare (seldom occurring) is opposite to being everywhere in the work.
Sparse (thinly distributed) is contrary to ubiquitous presence.
Isolated (standing alone or separate) opposes the everywhere-at-once quality.
Unique (the only one) is opposite to pervasive, repeated presence.
